fieldData.full-article-text:
“DAO” stands for decentralized autonomous organization. Like any organization, a DAO is a group of people with a set of common objectives.

However, unlike traditional organizations, DAOs are decentralized in a way that wasn’t possible prior to blockchain and DLT technologies. 

Before blockchain existed, any organization, even if it was as flat and democratic as it could possibly be, needed some form of hierarchy and trust. For example, the organization’s funds would have to be held in some sort of treasury, whether in a bank or under someone’s mattress. Trust would therefore have to be placed in certain individuals in the group. This, by definition, creates a form of hierarchy, as powers are not completely homogenous across the group.

A DAO, leveraging the permissionless and trustless nature of blockchain, tokens, and smart contracts, allows individuals to form organizations where no one person is in charge and where trust does not have to be placed in any other individual.

Instead, smart contracts and governance tokens can be used to make decisions without needing any central entity managing the process or controlling funds. Smart contracts can be set up to enforce business processes. Multisignature schemes can be used to authorize certain types of transactions only after a certain quorum of vote weight has approved it.

In short, DAOs offer a fundamentally different way of organizing human endeavors that have previously never been possible. They open up many new business models, incentive structures, and methods of governing.

When you hear DAOs referenced, you need to differentiate between the concept of a DAO, as described here, and “The DAO,” which is the name of a project that first attempted to create a DAO on Ethereum. It failed within a few months due to a mistake in its initial code, causing the loss of millions of Ether and eventually leading to the decision to hard fork Ethereum in 2016, resulting in the parallel “Ethereum Classic” blockchain.
